extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency officials, regulators, and practitioners interested in agency policymaking and procedural law
extracted.subtask_description: A law review discussion of when and why agencies should use adjudication rather than notice-and-comment rulemaking, describing adjudication’s benefits, legal limits, and the evolving judicial and procedural landscape that affects agency policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudicative Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication “grounds the agency’s decision-making in empirical reality” by requiring agencies to confront the facts of a case (so-called adjudicative facts) rather than largely hypothetical situations or cherry-picked examples provided by commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kenneth Culp Davis: adjudicative facts answer who/what/where/when/how/why and are the kinds of facts that go to a jury. Chenery II suggests agencies may lack experience to rigidify a tentative judgment into a rule but can gain experience through adjudication. Testimonial proof and cross-examination can be valuable in testing forecasts and generalized conclusions. Agencies in adjudication can observe concrete harms/benefits and emotional or historical context that might be lost in quantified cost–benefit analyses, which can average out or erase crucial moral or contextual considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex Post Clarification and Prospective Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication permits ex post clarification of policy and 'prospective flexibility'—agencies can address unforeseen problems in particular cases rather than trying to anticipate every scenario in a general rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems may arise that an agency could not reasonably foresee; requiring ex ante rulemakings risks facilitating evasion of statutory objectives. Adjudication allows agencies to leave questions unanswered, causing regulated entities to act cautiously (e.g., adhere to the strictest interpretation). But there are legal limits: under FCC v. Fox, notice must be given of a new policy so regulated parties 'should know what is required of them,' meaning some kinds of broad, novel obligations (e.g., an SEC requirement that all public companies fill a new quarterly form) would likely be improper to announce only via adjudication. Distinguish between permissible retroactive clarification of unsettled law and impermissible retroactive changes in settled law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-Case Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication allows agencies to develop policy slowly through the 'accumulation of experience in individual cases,' which can be better than articulating a general rule when problems are specialized or facts vary widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issues are new or too fact-specific for a general rule, agencies may 'develop policy realistically with actual problems' rather than relying on hypothetical cases. Case-by-case development is appropriate for issues 'so specialized and varying in nature as to be impossible of capture within the boundaries of a general rule.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent Policymaking Opportunities and Experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication provides more frequent opportunities to make policy—agencies can make policy every time a case arises—and thus can experiment and iterate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudication permits 'ability to experiment with limited adverse consequences' and to change policy swiftly if consequences differ from expectations. Agencies can incrementally develop regulatory regimes, refine categories from adjudicatory records, and learn from repeated exposure to an issue. Ensure procedural protections so subsequent non-agency parties do not face unfair surprise when policies evolve across adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Participation via Adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudications may create additional opportunities for public participation, particularly for communities and marginalized groups who may be more likely to engage in a concrete hearing about a specific facility or harm than in nationwide notice-and-comment rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice-and-comment has become technocratic and data-centric, often privileging sophisticated parties who can generate technical data; many affected communities lack resources to participate effectively in multiple rulemakings. Adjudication’s concreteness can mobilize community members and better surface harms and perspectives that rulemakings may ignore, though some groups may still lack resources to participate in repeated adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking Ossification and Time Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking procedures have 'ossified'—increases in judicial interpretation, legislation, and executive orders have layered procedural requirements that lengthen and complicate informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What began as comparatively simple procedures (APA §553 requiring a 'concise general statement of their basis and purpose') has become often book-length preambles and massive records. Examples: 1975 DOL notice three pages vs. later fiduciary rule preamble and exemptions totaling hundreds of pages; GAO findings that OSHA standard-setting averaged more than 7 years between 1981 and 2010. The cumulative effect is increased staff time and reluctance to undertake rulemakings frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Requirements Expanding Rule Preambles
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have created incentives for agencies to expand preambles and rulemaking records because expanded records can be used both to defend rules and to provide material for future challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preambles often function as 'massive lines of defense' constructed to protect rules from judicial challenge, rather than concise explanations for readers. Regulated parties may flood the record with material to preserve arguments for litigation. Even so, such defenses can fail; courts have criticized rulemaking records as a 'sump' of unrefined materials. Agencies often feel compelled to include extensive information to satisfy judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-1960s Deferential Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically (through the 1960s), courts applied an 'extremely deferential' standard to agency regulations; enforcement proceedings provided the factual record and courts would uphold agency policy so long as any conceivable state of facts could sustain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two rationales: much regulation was made via adjudication rather than rulemaking, and pre-enforcement review was rare. When enforcement produced a factual record, courts could examine application and were more tolerant of general regulatory statements. This contrasts with more searching modern review of rulemaking records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbott Laboratories — Pre-Enforcement Review Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbott Laboratories established that pre-enforcement review is generally available and that only 'clear and convincing evidence' of contrary legislative intent should bar judicial review, particularly where regulations 'require an immediate and significant change' with penalties attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbott transformed judicial review by permitting challenges to regulations before enforcement, which narrowed the evidentiary record available to courts and put pressure on courts to require agencies to flesh out their administrative records. This contributed to judicial demands that notice-and-comment records disclose underlying data and methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automotive Parts — Expectation for Detailed Preambles
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Circuit in Automotive Parts cautioned against a literal reading of APA terms 'concise' and 'general,' effectively expecting agency notices and preambles to reveal enough to enable meaningful judicial review of major policy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts expect a preamble that 'will enable us to see what major issues of policy were ventilated by the informal proceedings and why the agency reacted to them as it did.' This ruling has been read to justify extensive preambles; agencies cannot rely on literal concision to avoid addressing significant issues that courts will examine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous Rationales and Closed Administrative Record (Overton Park)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overton Park requires courts to look to the contemporaneous rationales of agencies and to base review on the 'full administrative record that was before the [agency] at the time' the decision was made, rejecting post-hoc rationalizations and affidavits as substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must thoroughly document their rationales at the time of decision-making; post-hoc litigation justifications are insufficient. Courts will generally refuse to consider extra-record evidence; reliance on affidavits or later explanations may be deemed inadequate, and failure to place reasoning in the record can be a fatal error on review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice Requirement for New Policies (FCC v. Fox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under FCC v. Fox, notice must be given of a new policy sufficient so that 'regulated parties should know what is required of them so they may act accordingly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal standard limits what policies can lawfully be articulated solely through adjudication: if a new, clear obligation is created, lack of prior notice to regulated parties may render adjudicative unilateral imposition improper. The article gives the example that courts would likely not permit the SEC to require all public companies to complete a new specific form via adjudication because the first defendant would lack advanced warning.
